newsitem.title: CANADA: Numac CEO says turnaround well under way.
newsitem.headline: Numac CEO says turnaround well under way.

text.p: Numac Energy Inc expected higher cash flow, earnings and production in 1997, a signal that its long-awaited turnaround was well under way, Chief Executive Stewart McGregor said on Thursday.

Numac, until recently speculated to be a takeover target, was projected to post 1997 cash flow of C$135 million or C$1.40 a share, up from C$122 million or C$1.30 a share last year, McGregor told the annual meeting.
Earnings were projected at C$18 million or C$0.19 a share, up from C$17 million or C$0.18 a share in 1996, he said.
Oil and gas liquids production was on target to average 20,700 barrels a day in 1997, up from 18,860 in 1996, he said.

Average natural gas output was estimated at 155 million cubic feet a day, a jump from 129 million last year, due largely to the company's C$133.6 million acquisition of Wainoco Oil Corp's Canadian assets earlier this month.

McGregor said, however, that Numac's turnaround -- fueled by a strategic shift to lower-risk projects -- had yet to be recognized by much of the investment community, resulting in its lackluster stock market performance.

The company has had a difficult time convincing analysts that it was recovering after a devastating 1995 that culminated in a C$179 million net loss, mostly from a big writedown of its reserves value.

The poor performance led to industry speculation that its major shareholder, a consortium of Hong Kong-based investors that holds 52 percent of the company, was aiming to put the company on the auction block.
"Historically, the company's performance has...caused the investment community to lose interest in the company to some extent. We've kind of been forgotten," McGregor said.
"I think it's a matter of clearly demonstrating that we are on the right track, that we are capable of adding reserves and production efficiently -- we're starting to show that," he said.
Numac shares were up 0.05 to 5.80 today in Toronto, about midway between its year low of 5.20 and high of 6.45.
McGregor said the stock price, which represented a multiple of just more than four times cash flow, valued the company below its net asset value.
He pegged Numac's value at C$6.75 a share using a 15 percent after-tax discount rate.
Much of the company's production growth over the next two years was expected to come from its Manitokan heavy oil play in Alberta, site of a multi-well drilling program, McGregor said.
Production at Manitokan, currently 1,900 barrels a day, was slated to rise to rise to 5,000 barrels a day in 1998 and 10,000 in 1999 by drilling 100 slant wells a year, he said.
About C$40 million of Numac's C$150 million 1997 capital budget was slated to be spent on the project.

The Wainoco purchase, which added production and acreage in northeast British Columbia and in Alberta, was expected to account for C$0.14 a share in cash flow and C$0.05 a share in earnings this year on an annualized basis, he said.

The company also hoped to net C$30 million from various non-core property sales this year, which would be targeted to reducing long-term debt to 1.5 times 1997 cash flow from the current 2.1 times, McGregor said.
